content: The Bogalusa Heart Study, published in Pediatrics in 2006, demonstrated the predictive value of childhood cardiovascular risk factors for adult dyslipidemia and other cardiovascular risks. Similarly, the Muscatine Study, published in Circulation in 2001, established a relationship between carotid intima-media thickness and cardiovascular risk factors measured from childhood through middle age. The Cardiovascular Risk in Young Finns Study, published in JAMA in 2003, further confirmed that childhood cardiovascular risk factors are associated with carotid artery intima-media thickness in adulthood. The Bogalusa Heart Study, also published in JAMA in 2003, highlighted the link between childhood cardiovascular risk factors and carotid vascular changes in adulthood. A systematic review and meta-analysis published in Circulation in 2007 by Lorenz et al. emphasized the predictive value of carotid intima-media thickness for clinical cardiovascular events. Research by Stein et al., published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 1982, explored the effects of dietary modifications on plasma lipid and lipoprotein fractions in children with normal and hypercholesterolemic profiles. Vartiainen et al., in a study published in Acta Paediatrica Scandinavica in 1986, examined the impact of dietary fat modifications on serum lipids and blood pressure in children. Stein et al., in a 1975 study published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, investigated the effects of natural and synthetic polyunsaturated foods on plasma cholesterol levels in adolescent males. Kaufmann et al., in a 1975 study published in Diabetes, examined the impact of a cholesteroland saturated fat-restricted diet on plasma lipid levels in diabetic children. McGandy et al., in a 1972 pilot study published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, explored dietary regulation of blood cholesterol in adolescent males. The WHO guidelines on saturated and trans-fatty acid intake for adults and children emphasize the importance of reducing these fats to improve cardiovascular health. Studies such as those by Hooper et al. (Cochrane Database, 2020) and Reynolds et al. (BMJ, 2015) systematically reviewed the effects of reducing saturated and trans-fat intake on cardiovascular disease risk. The STRIP (Special Turku Coronary Risk Factor Intervention Project) studies, published in journals such as Diabetes Care and JAMA, demonstrated that infancy-onset dietary counseling for a low-saturated-fat diet improves insulin sensitivity and cardiovascular risk factors in children and adolescents. These findings were supported by additional research on the neurological and behavioral development of children receiving low-saturated-fat diets. The DISC (Dietary Intervention Study in Children) studies, published in JAMA and the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, confirmed the efficacy and safety of reducing dietary fat and cholesterol intake in children with elevated LDL cholesterol. These studies also demonstrated that such interventions do not adversely affect psychological outcomes. Research by Hodson et al., published in Progress in Lipid Research in 2008, highlighted the use of fatty acid composition in adipose tissue and blood as biomarkers of dietary intake. Studies by Desroches et al. and Motard-Belanger et al., published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, examined the effects of dietary conjugated linoleic acids and trans-fatty acids on lipid profiles and cardiovascular risk factors. Gebauer et al., in a 2015 study published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, demonstrated the adverse effects of trans-fatty acid isomers on LDL cholesterol. Radtke et al., in a 2017 study published in the European Journal of Preventive Cardiology, explored the short-term effects of trans-fatty acids from ruminant and industrial sources on cardiovascular risk markers. The WHO's global trans-fat elimination initiative, as outlined in its 2022 report, emphasizes the importance of reducing trans-fat consumption to improve public health outcomes. Studies such as those by Downs et al. (Current Developments in Nutrition, 2020) and Marklund et al. (PLOS Medicine, 2020) evaluated the health benefits and cost-effectiveness of eliminating industrial trans-fatty acids. Socioeconomic factors and their impact on cardiovascular outcomes were explored in studies such as those by Schultz et al. (Circulation, 2018) and Allen et al. (Lancet Global Health, 2017). These studies highlighted the challenges and interventions needed to address cardiovascular risk in lowand middle-income countries. Finally, studies such as those by Jousilahti et al. (BMJ, 2016) and Vartiainen et al. (Global Heart, 2016) demonstrated the long-term benefits of primary prevention and risk factor reduction in reducing coronary heart disease mortality. The Danish saturated fat tax, as evaluated by Smed et al. (European Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 2016), provided insights into the effects of policy interventions on dietary intake and health outcomes.
